newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan foreign minister flies to Peru for crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan foreign minister flies to Peru for crisis.

text.p: Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda pledged before departing for Peru on Thursday his best efforts to help resolve the hostage crisis in the Japanese ambassador's residence there.

"It's a difficult situation, but our prime concern is to see that the hostages are released safely and we will do our best to see that the situation is quickly and peacefully resolved," Ikeda told reporters before leaving for Lima early Thursday afternoon.

Ikeda declined to reveal details of his mission due to the tense nature of the crisis, in which Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels stormed the Lima ambassador's residence on Tuesday and have threatened to kill some 485 hostages unless Peru releases up to 500 jailed comrades.
The hostages were attending a party to celebrate the 63rd birthday of Japan's Emperor Akihito next Monday.
"We will carefully observe the developments and take necessary action as the situation warrants," Ikeda said.

Ikeda also said that he met acting U.S. ambassador Rust Deming, who brought a letter from U.S. President Bill Clinton to Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto earlier on Thursday expressing concern over the situation and offering help.
While estimates by the government and released hostages put the number of captives between 200 and 300, a letter signed by the captives and faxed to relatives said the rebels were holding 490 men.
Among the some 120 Japanese hostages, 15 are embassy staff, including ambassador to Peru Morihisa Aoki, according to the Japanese Foreign Ministry.

Earlier, the leftist guerrillas, threatening to kill the hostages in the Japanese ambassador's residence, freed three ambassadors on Wednesday to negotiate the release of the captives in exchange for jailed rebels.

Hashimoto set up a special task force with eight cabinet members and the National Police Agency chief to deal with the crisis. Hashimoto, who said he will personally head the force, called the first meeting for Thursday afternoon.
